stories.topicLabel: Migrant crossings surge into Spain's Ceuta enclave
stories.analysis: Coverage of this story skewed notably rightward across all available headlines, with a bias spread of just one point between the least and most charged outlets. The Daily Mail, at the lower end, framed the story through implied governmental misalignment, contrasting "electric car chargers" spending with "250 more migrants arrive" — using the phrase "small boats crisis" to signal urgency without explicitly invoking threat language. Breitbart, at the far right of this sample, escalated significantly further, describing events as a "Migrant Invasion" and framing social media moderation as "Censorship of Supposed Disinfo" — language that recasts migration as military aggression and positions fact-checking institutions as adversaries. A second Breitbart headline reinforced this framing by pairing a statistical claim ("191% surge") with the phrase "before Invasion Began," treating the data as evidence of a coordinated attack. No centrist or left-leaning outlets appeared in this sample, so only the right end of the framing spectrum is represented.

stories.topicLabel: Cambridge professor Jason Arday faces academic fraud allegations
stories.analysis: Coverage of Jason Arday's fraud allegations spans roughly four points on the bias scale, reflecting genuinely different editorial angles. At the left end, the BBC leads with the Cambridge chancellor's voice, foregrounding the phrase "racist feeding frenzy" — language that casts critics as racially motivated attackers and positions Arday as a target rather than a subject of legitimate scrutiny. At the right end, The Free Press runs John McWhorter's framing, "How Academia Created Jason Arday," shifting moral responsibility away from Arday individually and toward institutional failures — a systemic critique common in conservative commentary on higher education. The Atlantic occupies a middle-right position with "Jason Arday's Final Self-Delusion," which is sharply critical of Arday personally through the dismissive phrase "self-delusion," yet also gestures toward broader academic culture. The core framing difference, then, is directional: the leftmost headline deflects scrutiny toward Arday's critics, while the rightmost redirects it toward the institutions that elevated him.

stories.topicLabel: White House aide Natalie Harp in spotlight amid Melania absence
stories.analysis: With a bias spread of just 1.0 points, coverage of this story was largely uniform, though Metro's headline introduced the most notable framing difference. By opening with the rhetorical question "Where's Melania Trump?" and noting that the president "is spotted everywhere with aide Natalie Harp," Metro implied a suspicious or scandalous dynamic, using Melania's absence as a hook rather than treating it as incidental context. The Wall Street Journal's reference to a "messy brawl" was more colorful but remained essentially descriptive of an internal conflict, while the Financial Times took the most straightforward approach, reporting plainly that a "ballroom official held quiet Kremlin talks" — a wire-style construction that made no attempt to sensationalize. The narrow spread across outlets reflects broad agreement on the basic facts; the main framing divergence was Metro's choice to frame proximity and absence as inherently suspicious.
